etymology: Hebrew qīr, “a wall” or “a fortress,” joined to Moab; the walled stronghold of Moab, also called Kir-haraseth and Kir-heres, “the city of the potsherds” or “the brick fortress.”
biblical_def: Kir of Moab was the chief fortress and stronghold of the Moabites, set high among their mountains and trusted in as their refuge. In the burden of Moab the prophet cries, “Because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence” (Isa 15:1); the strong city fell in a single night, that Moab might learn how vain is the wall a man builds against the LORD. It is named also Kirhareseth, for whose stricken foundations Moab is called to mourn (Isa 16:7), and Kirharesh, for which the prophet’s very bowels sound like an harp (Isa 16:11). When Israel and Judah came down against Moab, they beat down the cities and left Kirharaseth only the stones thereof, while the slingers compassed it about (2Ki 3:25). Jeremiah takes up the same lament: “mine heart shall mourn for the men of Kirheres” (Jer 48:31), and again, “mine heart shall sound like pipes for the men of Kirheres” (Jer 48:36). Here a proud people had settled on their lees (Jer 48:11), thinking their fortress sure. Yet the LORD brought down the high looks of Moab and laid the stronghold silent. Let the saint learn that no rampart of stone, no wealth long undisturbed, can stand when God ariseth to judge; the only sure fortress is the LORD Himself.
webster_summary: The chief fortress of Moab, called also Kir-haraseth and Kir-heres, laid waste in the night under the burden of the LORD.
webster_full: KIR OF MOAB, the walled stronghold and chief fortress of the Moabites, set among their mountains.
The name signifies “a wall” or “a fortress,” and it is called also Kir-haraseth, Kir-heres, and Kir-haraseth of the potsherds.
It was laid waste in the night under the burden of Moab pronounced by Isaiah.
When Israel and Judah warred against Moab, the slingers left it only the bare stones thereof.
It stands a witness that no fortress of man can stand against the judgment of the LORD.
scriptures: Isa 15:1
The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence;
Isa 16:7
Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kirhareseth shall ye mourn; surely they are stricken.

And they beat down the cities, and on every good piece of land cast every man his stone, and filled it; and they stopped all the wells of water, and felled all the good trees: only in Kirharaseth left they the stones thereof; howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it.
Therefore will I howl for Moab, and I will cry out for all Moab; mine heart shall mourn for the men of Kirheres.
corruption_summary: A fortress of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that no wall of man can stand when the LORD ariseth to judge a proud people.
corruption_paragraphs: Kir of Moab is named plainly in the burden of Moab as the trusted stronghold of a people grown proud and at ease. The sin that Scripture lays bare here is the pride of Moab, who settled on his lees and reckoned his fortress sure (Jer 48:11); the LORD answers that confidence by laying the wall waste in the night.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the vanity of every fleshly refuge and the sure foundation of those who trust the LORD. He breaketh down the high places of human pride that He may be the only fortress, rock, and refuge of His people; the man who builds his hope on Christ alone builds upon a stone that cannot be cast down.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “a wall” or “a fortress,” Kir of Moab names the walled stronghold of the Moabites laid silent under judgment.
roots_lines: Kir of Moab — Hebrew qīr, “a wall” or “a fortress,” joined to Moab.
It is called also Kir-haraseth and Kir-heres, the city of the potsherds or brick fortress.
It was the chief stronghold and refuge of the Moabite people.
Isaiah and Jeremiah alike take up a lament for its stricken foundations.
Israel and Judah left it only the bare stones thereof in the day of battle.
usage: Like Kir of Moab, every fortress of pride is laid silent in a night when the LORD ariseth to judge.
The saint flees not to a wall of stone but to the LORD, who is fortress, rock, and refuge.
Riches long undisturbed and ramparts long unbroken cannot stand against the burden of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew ‘arō‘ēr, “ruins” or “bare height,” with Arnon, “rushing stream”; the border city standing upon the very brink of the river Arnon.
biblical_def: Aroer by the Arnon was the southern border city of the Amorite kingdom of Sihon, perched upon the rim of the deep gorge of the river Arnon. When the LORD delivered Sihon before Israel, the conquest is measured “from Aroer, which is by the brink of the river of Arnon” (Deu 2:36); there was not one city too strong, for the LORD gave all into Israel’s hand. The land from Aroer was granted unto the Reubenites and the Gadites (Deu 3:12), and the inheritance of Reuben is marked again “from Aroer, that is upon the bank of the river Arnon” (Josh 13:16). Joshua records how Sihon “ruled from Aroer, which is upon the bank of the river Arnon” (Josh 12:2). In the day of Moab’s calamity Jeremiah calls upon her: “O inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way, and espy; ask him that fleeth, and her that escapeth, and say, What is done?” (Jer 48:19). This Aroer is to be distinguished from the Aroer before Rabbah given to Gad, and from the Aroer of Judah. It is a frontier stone, set where the river divides the land. Let it remind the believer that the LORD setteth the bounds of habitation (Deu 32:8); the borders of the nations and the lines of our heritage fall by His appointment, and the inheritance of His people is no chance possession but a gift of His covenant hand.
webster_summary: The border city upon the brink of the river Arnon, frontier of the Amorite kingdom, given to Reuben in Israel’s inheritance.
webster_full: AROER BY THE ARNON, the city standing upon the very brink of the deep gorge of the river Arnon.
The name signifies “ruins” or “bare height,” and it marked the southern frontier of Sihon the Amorite.
It became the boundary of the inheritance given to the tribe of Reuben.
It is to be distinguished from the Aroer of Gad before Rabbah and the Aroer of Judah.
It witnesses that the LORD setteth the bounds of habitation and divides the inheritance of His people.

corruption_summary: A border place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the LORD setteth the bounds of the nations and divides the inheritance of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Aroer by the Arnon is a frontier city of the sacred record, named where the river divides the land and the inheritance of Reuben begins. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it; the dictionary marks it that the reader may know it for a real boundary in a real land, distinct from the other Aroers of Gad and Judah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over the bounds of habitation (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). He who fixed the lip of the Arnon as a border, and gave the cities thereof to His people, orders still the lines that fall to us; the heritage of the saints is no accident of history but the appointment of a covenant-keeping God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “ruins” or “bare height,” Aroer names the city set upon the brink of the river Arnon.

etymology: Hebrew bāmōth ba‘al, “the high places of Baal,” from bāmāh, a height or high place, joined to Baal, the lord; an elevated site of idolatrous worship in the land of Moab.
biblical_def: Bamoth-baal, “the high places of Baal,” was a height in the land of Moab whither Balak the king of Moab brought Balaam, that from thence he might see and curse the people of God: “Balak took Balaam, and brought him up into the high places of Baal, that thence he might see the utmost part of the people” (Num 22:41). The very name confesses what was done upon those summits, for the high places were the seats of the false worship of Baal, the idol-lord of Canaan and Moab. In the dividing of the land the place is named among the cities of Reuben: “Dibon, and Bamothbaal, and Bethbaalmeon” (Josh 13:17). It is to be remembered together with the station called simply Bamoth in Israel’s journeyings (Num 21:19), a height in the valley of Moab near the top of Pisgah (Num 21:20). Here the Scripture names the idolatry of the high places plainly: men climbed to the heights to worship the work of their own hands, and Balak hoped that from such a place divination might prevail against the LORD’s elect. Yet God turned the curse into a blessing, for none can curse whom He hath blessed. Let the saint abhor the high places of Baal in every age, and worship the living God alone, who will not give His glory to another, nor His people into the hand of the enchanter.
webster_summary: A height in Moab, the high places of Baal, whither Balak brought Balaam to behold and curse the people of God.
webster_full: BAMOTH-BAAL, a height in the land of Moab whose name signifies “the high places of Baal.”
The high places were the seats of the idolatrous worship of Baal, the false lord of Canaan and Moab.
Thither Balak the king of Moab brought Balaam, that he might see and curse the people of God.
It is named among the cities of Reuben, with Dibon and Beth-baal-meon.
It witnesses that God turneth the curse into a blessing and will not give His people into the enchanter’s hand.
scriptures: And it came to pass on the morrow, that Balak took Balaam, and brought him up into the high places of Baal, that thence he might see the utmost part of the people.

Heshbon, and all her cities that are in the plain; Dibon, and Bamothbaal, and Bethbaalmeon,
And from Mattanah to Nahaliel: and from Nahaliel to Bamoth:
And from Bamoth in the valley, that is in the country of Moab, to the top of Pisgah, which looketh toward Jeshimon.
corruption_summary: A high place of Baal named plainly in Scripture as a seat of idolatry; it witnesses that God turneth the curse into a blessing upon His chosen.
corruption_paragraphs: Bamoth-baal is no neutral hilltop but, by its own name, “the high places of Baal,” a seat of false worship in Moab. Scripture names the corruption plainly: the idolatry of the high places, where men climbed to bow before the work of their own hands, and whither Balak brought a hireling prophet hoping that divination might prevail against the LORD’s people. This is the sin the height confesses, and the dictionary names it in Scripture’s own vocabulary — idolatry, false worship, the lust to curse what God hath blessed.

The principle to recover is that the LORD will not give His glory to another, nor His elect into the hand of the enchanter. From the high places of Baal no curse could fall upon Israel, for God turned it into a blessing (Deu 23:5). The high places must come down; the saint worships the living God alone, and rests secure that none can lay anything to the charge of God’s elect, for it is God that justifieth.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the high places of Baal,” Bamoth-baal names an idolatrous height in the land of Moab.

etymology: Hebrew nēbō, perhaps “height” or “prophet”; a summit of the Abarim range in Moab, the top of Pisgah over against Jericho, whence Moses beheld the promised land.
biblical_def: Mount Nebo was the height in the land of Moab, a peak of the Abarim, called also the top of Pisgah, over against Jericho, whence the LORD shewed Moses the land of promise before he died. The LORD said unto him, “Get thee up into this mountain Abarim, unto mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, that is over against Jericho; and behold the land of Canaan” (Deu 32:49). And Moses went up “from the plains of Moab unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. And the LORD shewed him all the land” (Deu 34:1). There the servant of the LORD looked upon the inheritance he might not enter, and there he died: “So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD” (Deu 34:5). And the LORD Himself buried him in a valley in Moab, over against Bethpeor, “but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). This Nebo is to be distinguished from the Moabite town Nebo and from the idol Nebo that stoopeth in Babylon (Isa 46:1). Upon this height the law-giver was gathered to his people as Aaron was upon mount Hor. Let the believer learn that the faithful servant may see the promise from afar and yet be carried home before its full possession; for there is a better country, and a Joshua greater than Moses who brings His people in. The grave of Moses, hid by God’s own hand, preaches that the saint’s end is in the keeping of the LORD.
webster_summary: The summit of Pisgah in Moab, over against Jericho, whence Moses beheld the promised land and there died and was buried by the LORD.
webster_full: MOUNT NEBO, a height of the Abarim range in the land of Moab, called also the top of Pisgah.
It stood over against Jericho, whence the LORD shewed Moses all the land of promise.
There Moses the servant of the LORD died, according to the word of the LORD.
The LORD Himself buried him in a valley over against Bethpeor, and no man knoweth his sepulchre.
It is to be distinguished from the town of Nebo and from the idol Nebo of Babylon.

Deu 34:6
And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.
corruption_summary: A holy height of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the faithful servant may behold the promise from afar and rest his end wholly in the keeping of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Mount Nebo is the height where Moses beheld the land and died, and no movement of the present age has set itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may distinguish this holy summit from the Moabite town Nebo and from the idol Nebo that stoopeth in Babylon (Isa 46:1), and may stand in awe at the grave God hid with His own hand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD keeps both the labour and the end of His servants. Moses might see the inheritance from Pisgah yet not enter it, for a greater than Moses must bring the people in; and the believer, who shall die before the full possession of the promise, looks to the resurrection and the better country, his sepulchre and his hope alike in the hand of God.

etymology: Hebrew pē‘ōr, “a cleft” or “opening,” a height in Moab; bound up with Baal-peor, the idol worshipped upon it, and with Israel’s whoredom there.
biblical_def: Peor was a height of Moab, “the top of Peor, that looketh toward Jeshimon” (Num 23:28), whither Balak brought Balaam for the third and last attempt to curse Israel. The place is forever bound up with the shame that followed: there Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor, the idol of that mountain, and “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel” (Num 25:3). The men of Israel went a whoring after the daughters of Moab and Midian, were drawn into the worship of their god, and a plague brake out among the congregation, until Phinehas the son of Eleazar, in holy zeal, turned away the wrath of God. Long after, the elders remember it: “Is the iniquity of Peor too little for us, from which we are not cleansed until this day” (Josh 22:17). Moses charges that the Midianites “beguiled you in the matter of Peor” (Num 25:18), and that the counsel of Balaam wrought this trespass against the LORD (Num 31:16). Here the Scripture names the corruption plainly: idolatry and whoredom, the doubled sin of the high place. Yet the zeal of Phinehas and the swift judgment of God stand as a warning and a mercy. Let the believer flee both idolatry and uncleanness, for the LORD is a jealous God; and let him bless the Mediator whose zeal for His Father’s house, and whose blood, turn away a greater wrath than the plague of Peor.
webster_summary: A height in Moab whither Balak brought Balaam, bound up with Baal-peor, Israel’s whoredom, the plague, and the zeal of Phinehas.
webster_full: PEOR, a height of Moab, the top that looketh toward Jeshimon, whither Balak brought Balaam.
Upon it was worshipped Baal-peor, the idol whose name the mountain bears.
There Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor and went a whoring after the daughters of Moab.
The anger of the LORD was kindled, and a plague brake out, until Phinehas turned away His wrath.
It witnesses against the doubled sin of idolatry and uncleanness, and the jealousy of a holy God.
scriptures: And Balak brought Balaam unto the top of Peor, that looketh toward Jeshimon.
Num 25:3
And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.

For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, which was slain in the day of the plague for Peor's sake.
Josh 22:17
Is the iniquity of Peor too little for us, from which we are not cleansed until this day, although there was a plague in the congregation of the LORD,
corruption_summary: A high place of Moab where Israel fell into idolatry and whoredom; Scripture names the doubled sin plainly and sets the zeal of Phinehas against it.
corruption_paragraphs: Peor is no mere place-name but the scene of a notorious corruption that Scripture refuses to gloss. Upon this height Baal-peor was worshipped, and there Israel joined himself to the idol and went a whoring after the daughters of Moab (Num 25:3). The dictionary names the sin in Scripture’s own words — idolatry and uncleanness, the wiles of Balaam’s counsel, the trespass that kindled the anger of the LORD and brought a plague upon the camp.

The principle to recover is the jealousy of a holy God and the way of atonement. The plague was stayed not by indulgence but by the zeal of Phinehas, who stood up and executed judgment. So the saint must mortify both idolatry and lust, knowing the LORD will not share His glory; and he must look to the true Mediator, whose zeal and whose blood turn away a wrath greater than the plague of Peor, and cleanse the iniquity from which Israel could not cleanse herself.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “a cleft” or “opening,” Peor names a height of Moab bound up with the idol Baal-peor.

usage: Let the believer flee both idolatry and uncleanness, for the LORD at Peor is a jealous God.

etymology: Hebrew lūchīth, perhaps “of boards” or “tablets,” an ascent in the land of Moab; the going up of Luhith, climbed with weeping in the day of calamity.
biblical_def: Luhith was an ascent, a steep going up, in the land of Moab, named in the burden of Moab as a way of flight and weeping when judgment fell. Isaiah cries, “by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction” (Isa 15:5). The fugitives of Moab climbed that slope with continual lamentation, fleeing the spoiler. Jeremiah takes up the same word: “For in the going up of Luhith continual weeping shall go up; for in the going down of Horonaim the enemies have heard a cry of destruction” (Jer 48:5). The ascent of Luhith and the descent of Horonaim are set together, the one a climb of tears, the other a fall into ruin. Moab, who had been at ease from his youth and settled on his lees (Jer 48:11), now goes up weeping. Here is the wages of a proud people brought down: the very heights become highways of sorrow. Yet the prophet who pronounces the burden also weeps with them, for the LORD takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. Let the believer mark how surely judgment overtakes the secure and the proud, and let him climb a better ascent — the hill of the LORD, with clean hands and a pure heart, in repentance and not in vain mourning, that he may not be found at last among the weeping of the lost.
webster_summary: An ascent in the land of Moab, the going up of Luhith, climbed with continual weeping in the day of Moab’s calamity.
webster_full: LUHITH, a steep ascent in the land of Moab, named in the burden of Moab.
Its going up was climbed with continual weeping by the fugitives of Moab.
It is set in the prophets against the going down of Horonaim.
It marks the way of flight when the spoiler came upon a people at ease.
It witnesses that judgment overtakes the secure, and the heights become highways of sorrow.

Jer 48:5

Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.
Isa 16:6
We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is very proud: even of his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath: but his lies shall not be so.
corruption_summary: An ascent of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses against the false ease of the proud and the certain coming of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Luhith is a slope in the land of Moab, named only as a way of weeping flight under the burden of the LORD. No movement of the present age has set itself to redefine it; the dictionary records it that the reader may see, in the going up of Luhith, the sorrow appointed to a people grown proud and at ease.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that judgment surely overtakes the secure and the proud (Jer 48:11; Isa 16:6). Moab settled on his lees and was never emptied, yet at last he climbed the heights weeping. Let the believer not trust an undisturbed ease, but climb the hill of the LORD in repentance, with clean hands and a pure heart, lest he be found among the weeping of the lost.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew perhaps for “of boards” or “tablets,” Luhith names a steep ascent in Moab climbed with weeping.
roots_lines: Luhith — Hebrew lūchīth, perhaps “of boards” or “tablets.”

It is named in the burdens of Moab by both Isaiah and Jeremiah.
usage: Let no believer trust the undisturbed ease that Moab knew, lest he climb at last the going up of Luhith in tears.
Judgment overtakes the proud and secure as surely as the spoiler came upon Moab.

etymology: Hebrew chōrōnayim, “two caverns” or “two hollows,” a city of Moab; the place of a going down and a cry of destruction in the burden of Moab.
biblical_def: Horonaim was a city of Moab, set upon a descent, from which arose the cry of destruction in the day of the LORD’s judgment upon that land. Isaiah names it with Luhith: “in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction” (Isa 15:5). Jeremiah hears the same lament: “A voice of crying shall be from Horonaim, spoiling and great destruction” (Jer 48:3), and again, “in the going down of Horonaim the enemies have heard a cry of destruction” (Jer 48:5). The ascent of Luhith was climbed with weeping; the descent of Horonaim resounded with the shriek of ruin. The whole burden gathers up the howling of a stricken people, for the LORD had risen to bring down the pride of Moab. Moab had trusted in his works and in his treasures (Jer 48:7), and Chemosh his god could not deliver him; the cry from Horonaim is the sound of false confidence broken. Yet this same burden of Moab holds out a ray of mercy: “in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David” (Isa 16:5). Where the cry of destruction goes up from Moab, the promise of a righteous King in David’s line shines through. Let the believer hear in Horonaim the certain end of every refuge but Christ, and flee to the throne of mercy where alone the cry of the broken is answered with grace.
webster_summary: A city of Moab upon a descent, from which arose the cry of destruction and spoiling in the burden of Moab.
webster_full: HORONAIM, a city of Moab set upon a going down or descent.
Its name signifies “two caverns” or “two hollows.”
From it arose the cry of destruction and spoiling in the day of judgment.
It is set in the prophets against the going up of Luhith.
It witnesses that every refuge but the LORD ends in a cry of ruin.

My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction.
Jer 48:3
A voice of crying shall be from Horonaim, spoiling and great destruction.
Jer 48:7
For because thou hast trusted in thy works and in thy treasures, thou shalt also be taken: and Chemosh shall go forth into captivity with his priests and his princes together.

corruption_summary: A city of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that false confidence ends in a cry of ruin, while mercy is offered through a King in David’s line.
corruption_paragraphs: Horonaim is a city of Moab named only in the burden of Moab as a place of the cry of destruction. No movement of the present age has troubled to redefine it; the dictionary records it that the reader may hear, in the voice of crying from Horonaim, the sound of a false confidence broken when the LORD arose to judge.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every trust but the LORD ends in ruin, yet mercy is held forth even in judgment. Moab trusted in his works and his treasures, and Chemosh could not deliver (Jer 48:7); but the same burden promises a throne established in mercy in the tabernacle of David (Isa 16:5). Let the believer flee from every Horonaim of false refuge to the throne of grace, where the cry of the broken is answered by a righteous King.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “two caverns” or “two hollows,” Horonaim names a city of Moab upon a descent of ruin.
roots_lines: Horonaim — Hebrew chōrōnayim, “two caverns” or “two hollows.”
It was a city of Moab set upon a going down or descent.
From it arose the cry of destruction and great spoiling.
It is set against the going up of Luhith in the prophets.
It is named in the burdens of Moab by both Isaiah and Jeremiah.
usage: Let the believer hear in Horonaim the certain end of every refuge but Christ.
False confidence in works and treasures ends, like Moab’s, in a cry of destruction.
Even amid the burden, mercy is offered through a throne established in the tabernacle of David.

etymology: Hebrew qiryāthayim, “double city” or “two cities,” from qiryāh, a city; a city of the plain built by Reuben, fallen again to Moab and brought under judgment.
biblical_def: Kiriathaim was a city of the level plateau east of Jordan, builded by the children of Reuben when they took their inheritance: “the children of Reuben built Heshbon, and Elealeh, and Kirjathaim” (Num 32:37). It is named among Reuben’s cities in the dividing of the land, “Kirjathaim, and Sibmah, and Zarethshahar in the mount of the valley” (Josh 13:19). In time it fell again into the hand of Moab, and so came under the LORD’s judgment with the rest of that land: “Woe unto Nebo! for it is spoiled: Kiriathaim is confounded and taken” (Jer 48:1). Ezekiel too marks it among the cities of Moab’s frontier given over to the children of the east: “Bethjeshimoth, Baalmeon, and Kiriathaim” (Eze 25:9). Thus a city once raised by a tribe of Israel passed to a heathen people and shared their fall, that none might presume upon a name once holy. The history of Kiriathaim preaches that a place, like a soul, may begin within the covenant and yet be lost to idolatry and pride if the LORD be forsaken. Let the believer hold fast his inheritance with reverence, build upon the true foundation, and not, like the cities of Reuben that drifted into Moab, exchange the worship of the living God for the high places of the heathen. What is once given of grace must be kept by grace, or it is taken and confounded.
webster_summary: A city of the plain built by Reuben, fallen again to Moab and brought under the LORD’s judgment with the rest of that land.
webster_full: KIRIATHAIM OF MOAB, a city of the level plateau east of Jordan, whose name signifies “double city.”
It was builded by the children of Reuben when they received their inheritance.
It is named among Reuben’s cities in the dividing of the land under Joshua.
In time it fell again to Moab and came under the LORD’s judgment.
It witnesses that a place once within the covenant may be lost to idolatry if the LORD be forsaken.

corruption_paragraphs: Kiriathaim is a city of the plain, builded by Reuben and afterward fallen to Moab, named under the LORD’s judgment. No movement of the present age has troubled to redefine it; the dictionary records it that the reader may mark a place once raised by a tribe of Israel which drifted into a heathen people’s pride and idolatry, and so was confounded and taken.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what is given of grace must be kept by grace. Reuben built the city, but it slipped to Moab and shared Moab’s fall; so the soul that presumes upon a name once holy, yet forsakes the LORD for the high places, is confounded. Let the believer hold fast his inheritance with reverence and build upon the true foundation alone.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “double city,” Kiriathaim names a city of the plain built by Reuben and judged with Moab.
roots_lines: Kiriathaim of Moab — Hebrew qiryāthayim, “double city” or “two cities.”
It is from qiryāh, a city, in a dual form.
It was a city of the level plateau builded by the children of Reuben.
It fell again to Moab and was confounded and taken under judgment.
It is named among Moab’s frontier cities by Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
usage: Let the believer hold fast his inheritance, lest like Kiriathaim it slip from the covenant to the heathen.
What is given of grace must be kept by grace, or it is confounded and taken away.
A name once holy is no safety where the LORD is forsaken for the high places.

etymology: Hebrew bēth diblathāyim, “house of the two cakes of figs,” from bēth, a house, and dēbēlāh, a cake of pressed figs; a city of Moab under the LORD’s judgment.
biblical_def: Beth-diblathaim was a city of Moab, named in Jeremiah’s burden among the towns brought under the judgment of the LORD: “And upon Dibon, and upon Nebo, and upon Bethdiblathaim” (Jer 48:22). Its name, “house of the two cakes of figs,” speaks of a land of fruitfulness and plenty, yet that very fatness could not shield it in the day of wrath. It is to be remembered together with the station of Israel’s journeyings called Almon-diblathaim, where the camp pitched after Dibon-gad: “they removed from Dibongad, and encamped in Almondiblathaim” (Num 33:46). The two names share the root of the fig-cake, marking a region of orchards and ease. But Moab had been at ease from his youth and settled on his lees (Jer 48:11), and the LORD swept the burden of Moab from city to city, sparing neither the fruitful nor the strong. Beth-diblathaim is one stone in that long roll of judgment, a witness that plenty is no defense against the holy God when a people grow proud in their abundance. Let the believer who enjoys the LORD’s temporal mercies not settle on his lees nor trust the fatness of his portion, but hold his abundance with a humble and thankful heart; for the houses of figs and the cities of plenty pass away, and only what is built upon the LORD endureth.
webster_summary: A city of Moab named under Jeremiah’s judgment, its name speaking of plenty that could not shield it in the day of wrath.

It witnesses that plenty is no defense against the holy God when a people grow proud.

corruption_paragraphs: Beth-diblathaim is a city of Moab named only in a roll of judgment, its very name speaking of fig-cakes and abundance. No movement of the present age has troubled to redefine it; the dictionary records it that the reader may see how a house of plenty was swept up with the proud cities of Moab in the day of the LORD’s wrath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that abundance breeds no safety where the heart grows proud and at ease (Jer 48:11; Jer 48:7). Moab trusted in his treasures, and the house of figs fell with the rest. Let the believer hold his temporal mercies with a humble and thankful heart, building upon the LORD alone, for the cities of plenty pass away and only His house endureth.

etymology: Hebrew qēriyōth, “cities” or “the towns,” the plural of qiryāh, a city; a fortified city of Moab whose palaces the fire of the LORD should devour.
biblical_def: Kerioth was a city of Moab, reckoned among her chief strongholds, whose palaces were marked for the devouring fire of the LORD’s judgment. Amos sets it at the head of the burden against Moab: “I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the palaces of Kerioth” (Amo 2:2); and Moab should die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet. Jeremiah names it in his great burden of Moab’s towns: “And upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near” (Jer 48:24); and again, “Kerioth is taken, and the strong holds are surprised” (Jer 48:41), so that the hearts of the mighty men of Moab should be as the heart of a woman in her pangs. This Kerioth is to be distinguished from Kerioth-hezron in the south of Judah (Josh 15:25). Its palaces were the pride and glory of Moab, and against that pride the LORD sent fire; for “we have heard the pride of Moab; he is very proud” (Isa 16:6). The strong holds men reckoned impregnable were surprised in a day, and the courage of the mighty melted away. Let the believer learn that the palaces of human pride are fuel for the fire of God, and that no fortress of stone or pomp of wealth can stand when He ariseth. The wise man builds not upon the high looks of Moab, but bows low before the King who sitteth in mercy upon the throne of David.
webster_summary: A fortified city of Moab whose palaces the fire of the LORD should devour, its strong holds surprised in the day of judgment.

corruption_summary: A city of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the palaces of human pride are fuel for the fire of God and no fortress can stand against Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Kerioth is a stronghold of Moab named in the prophets only under judgment, its palaces marked for the devouring fire of the LORD. No movement of the present age has troubled to redefine it; yet the sin Scripture sets against it is plain — the pride of Moab, very proud in his haughtiness and his wrath (Isa 16:6). The dictionary names that pride in Scripture’s own words, the high looks against which the fire was sent.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God bringeth down the proud and burns the palaces of human glory. Moab’s strong holds were surprised in a day and the mighty melted like a woman in her pangs; so falls every fortress of pomp and wealth that exalts itself against the LORD. The wise man builds not on the high looks of Moab but bows before the King who sitteth in mercy upon the throne of David (Isa 16:5).
